about.title: The Late 1960s and 1970s: Protest, War and Oil
about.length_note: About 30 minutes. Seven topics fit in a half-hour class because each idea gets short steps and a quick check. The Cultural Revolution debate gets the most time, since the course asks for the other side to be heard. The feminist and environmental sections follow US-focused sources, and the lesson says so. The frame of reference only lists events I could confirm in the sources I read, so some famous events are left out for now.

say.text: Welcome to class 58. Last time we looked at the 1950s and early 1960s. Today we cover about fifteen restless years, from 1966 to 1979.

show.text: The Late 1960s and 1970s: Protest, War and Oil

say.text: We will take five stories, one at a time. There is no rush, and I will check in with a question now and then.

show.text: 1. The Vietnam War; 2. The protests of 1968; 3. China's Cultural Revolution; 4. Middle East wars and the oil shock; 5. Environmental and women's movements

say.text: First, the Vietnam War. Vietnam was split into North and South in 1954. American involvement lasted about 25 years, from 1950 to 1975.
The war was between North and South Vietnam, and the United States backed the South. In the end, communist forces won, in 1975.

show.text: North Vietnam: communist-led | South Vietnam: backed by the United States

say.text: On January 31, 1968, about 70,000 northern troops began the Tet Offensive. Tet is the lunar new year.
Tet was a wave of coordinated attacks on more than 100 cities and towns in South Vietnam.

ask.right: A coordinated series of attacks on more than 100 cities and towns in South Vietnam
wrong: A peace treaty signed in Paris
A United States invasion of North Vietnam
ask.why: Tet began on January 31, 1968, when about 70,000 northern troops attacked more than 100 cities and towns.

say.text: The North hoped Tet would push the United States to the bargaining table. Most of its predictions did not come true.
Even so, peace talks between the US and North Vietnam opened in Paris that May. They went on for years.

show.text: 1968 January: Tet Offensive; 1968 May: talks open in Paris

say.text: The Paris Peace Accords were signed on January 27, 1973. They ended the American military role in the war.
But the war between North and South went on. On April 30, 1975, northern forces captured Saigon, the southern capital.

show.text: 1973: Paris Peace Accords; 1975 April 30: Saigon captured

ask.q: After the Paris Peace Accords, did the fighting between North and South Vietnam stop at once?
ask.right: No. It continued until Saigon was captured on April 30, 1975.
wrong: Yes. The war ended in 1973 and nothing more happened.
Yes. Saigon was captured the same day the accords were signed.
No. The fighting stopped in 1968, before the accords.
ask.why: The accords ended the American military role, but North and South kept fighting until Saigon fell in 1975.

say.text: Afterwards Vietnam was reunited, and Saigon was renamed Ho Chi Minh City. Ho himself had died in 1969.

show.text: A famous 1975 photograph: people on a Saigon rooftop climbing a ladder to a helicopter, April 29, 1975

say.text: At home, opposition to the war bitterly divided Americans. And the war was lighting fires far from Vietnam.
In 1968, waves of protest rolled through many countries. They included Brazil, Czechoslovakia, France, Mexico, Poland, South Africa and the US.

show.text: Brazil; Czechoslovakia; France; Mexico; Northern Ireland; Poland; Senegal; South Africa; Spain; United States

say.text: The causes varied: civil rights, racial and economic justice, and an end to rule without freedom.
Why students? In the 1960s, mass university education arrived. A radical youth culture came with it, and Vietnam became a trigger.

show.text: New: huge universities, youth culture | Trigger: the war in Vietnam

say.text: In France, protests began at Nanterre, a university near Paris. On May 3, 1968 they spilled into the Sorbonne in Paris.
One famous slogan of those weeks was 'it is forbidden to forbid'.

show.text: Il est interdit d'interdire! ('it is forbidden to forbid')

say.text: Then workers joined in. By May 22, nine million were on strike. It was France's largest general strike of the 20th century.

ask.q: Which group joined the students in Paris and turned the protests into a general strike?
ask.why: About nine million workers were on strike by May 22, making it France's largest general strike of the century.

say.text: Now to Czechoslovakia. On January 5, 1968, Alexander Dubcek became head of the Communist Party there.
He offered 'socialism with a human face'. That meant looser censorship and more open debate.

show.text: Looser censorship; more debate; reform from inside the Communist Party

ask.q: What did Dubcek's Prague Spring offer people?
ask.right: Looser censorship and more open debate
ask.why: Dubcek loosened censorship and expanded debate, and called it socialism with a human face.

say.text: It did not last. Soviet and allied armies invaded and crushed the resistance with force.

show.text: Prague Spring crushed by foreign armies

say.text: In Paris, Chicago, Berlin, Mexico City and Tokyo, forces of order also put down the budding revolts. In the US, 1968 deeply divided the public.

show.text: Paris; Chicago; Berlin; Mexico City; Tokyo

say.text: Now to China. There, young people were not protesting against the country's leader. The leader mobilized them. Warning: this part includes violence, and we will keep it calm and factual.
It is officially called the Great Proletarian Cultural Revolution. It ran from 1966 to 1976. Mao Zedong launched it to renew the spirit of revolution.
It was declared on May 16, 1966 and formally launched that August, with a first focus on schools and universities.
Why? Mao feared a new elite forming in China. He also thought his colleagues lacked commitment after the failed Great Leap Forward.

show.text: Mao's fear: a new elite | Mao's doubt: colleagues not committed

say.text: Mao organized young city people into groups called Red Guards. He shut the schools and urged them to attack traditional values.
They were told to root out anyone not 'sufficiently revolutionary', or suspected of being 'bourgeois'. There may have been as many as 11 million Red Guards.

ask.right: Groups of young people mobilized by Mao to attack traditional values and 'suspect' people
wrong: A secret police force run by teachers
ask.why: Mao organized urban youths into Red Guards, shut schools, and urged them to attack traditional values.

say.text: Teachers, educators, intellectuals and traditionalists were persecuted. Many were killed.
The Red Guards then split into factions. Each claimed to be the true voice of Mao.
By early 1967 top leaders wanted a halt. The army took over schools, factories and offices. Millions of Red Guards were sent out of the cities.
The Red Guard phase is dated from mid-1966 to early 1969. But the Cultural Revolution did not end there.

show.text: Mid-1966 to early 1969: Red Guard phase

say.text: From mid-1973 to Mao's death, politics swung between two groups. One was Jiang Qing's, later called the Gang of Four. The other was Zhou Enlai and Deng Xiaoping's.

show.text: Gang of Four (Jiang Qing and allies) | Zhou Enlai and Deng Xiaoping

say.text: Mao died on September 9, 1976. The Gang of Four was arrested in October. The Party officially declared it over in August 1977.

show.text: 1976 Sept 9: Mao dies; 1976 Oct: Gang of Four purged; 1977 Aug: officially over

ask.q: When did the Cultural Revolution really come to an end?
ask.right: In 1976, with Mao's death and the fall of the Gang of Four. It was officially declared over in 1977.
wrong: In 1969, when the Red Guard phase ended
ask.why: The Red Guard phase ended around 1969, but the upheaval continued until Mao died and the Gang of Four fell in 1976.

say.text: Now the debate: how should we assess the toll? Experts agree that many people died. They disagree about how many.

show.text: Debate: How Do We Count the Toll?

say.text: One reason is that records are hard to reach. Scholars struggle to get access to 'state secrets'.

Published estimates run from about 40,000 up to 8 million. Sociologist Andrew Walder says the low ones came from official party statements. He says the high ones were guesses by people angered by the politics.

show.text: Estimates of Cultural Revolution deaths, in millions

say.text: Careful studies narrow it. Walder used about 1,500 Chinese county records. He estimates 1.6 million deaths, but only for 1966 to 1969.
Other historians, such as Song Yongyi, say probably 2 to 3 million. Britannica gives a range of 500,000 to 2 million.

show.text: Walder: 1.6 million (1966-69); Song and others: about 2-3 million; Britannica: 0.5-2 million

ask.q: Why can't historians give one single number for the deaths?
ask.right: Records are hard to reach, and researchers use different methods and cover different years.
wrong: Because historians refuse to count deaths
Because one office published every number on the same day
Because nobody has ever studied it
ask.why: Records are state secrets, and studies differ in method and years covered. Walder's number, for example, only covers 1966 to 1969.

say.text: Deaths are not the whole toll. Millions were displaced, and the economy was badly disrupted.
After 1976, nearly three million party members, and many others wrongly purged, waited to be reinstated.
Who was responsible? Jiang Qing was arrested after Mao died and convicted in 1981.
Yet it remains unclear which big decisions were Mao's and which came from the Gang's own planning. That is another open question.
Now the Middle East. Let's go back to 1967 first.

show.text: The Middle East: Wars and Oil

say.text: The Six-Day War was fought from June 5 to 10, 1967, between Israel and Egypt, Jordan and Syria.

Tension had been rising. Egypt's Nasser used harsh words and mobilized troops. Israel then struck the Egyptian air force first, and the Jordanian, Syrian and Iraqi air forces later that day, in what Israel called a 'preemptive' attack.
A UN-brokered ceasefire took effect on June 10. By then Israel held a lot of new land.
Israel took the Sinai and Gaza from Egypt. It took the West Bank and East Jerusalem from Jordan, and the Golan Heights from Syria.

show.text: Map of Israel and neighbours showing Sinai and Gaza (from Egypt), West Bank and East Jerusalem (from Jordan), Golan Heights (from Syria)

ask.q: Which territory did Israel take from Egypt in 1967?
ask.right: The Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza Strip
ask.why: Israel took the Sinai and Gaza from Egypt. The Golan Heights came from Syria and the West Bank from Jordan.

say.text: Who was to blame for the war? Historians differ. Many accounts call Israel's strike preemptive.
Abba Eban, Israel's own foreign minister, later wrote that Nasser did not want war. Historian Martin van Creveld argued that Israel's forces were ready to provoke one.

show.text: Preemptive strike against rising threat | Israel's side also pushed toward war

say.text: Six years later, on October 6, 1973, Egypt under Sadat and Syria under Assad attacked Israel together. That was the Yom Kippur War.
The war lasted twenty days. But an oil embargo that grew out of it lasted five months.
OPEC is the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries. Its Arab members used oil as a political weapon.
An embargo means refusing to ship to certain countries. These Arab states stopped oil shipments as payback for support of Israel.
On October 17, 1973, Arab oil producers cut production by five percent. The same day they began an embargo against the United States.

show.text: 1973 Oct 17: production cut 5%, embargo on US begins

say.text: The embargo also targeted Canada, Japan, the Netherlands, Portugal, Rhodesia, South Africa and the United Kingdom. It lasted until March 1974.

show.text: Canada; Japan; Netherlands; Portugal; Rhodesia; South Africa; United Kingdom; United States

ask.q: Why did Arab OPEC members cut off oil to the United States and others in 1973?
ask.right: To pressure countries that supported Israel in the Yom Kippur War
wrong: To help Vietnam win its war
To protect their oil wells from storms
ask.why: The embargo was a response to support for Israel during the Yom Kippur War.

say.text: Oil prices shot up: 70 percent in October, then another 130 percent in December.
One source puts the total jump near 300 percent. There were shortages, and some refineries and industries shut down.
The shock showed how much industrial countries relied on imported oil. America responded by producing more at home and developing energy-saving technology.

show.text: Problem: heavy reliance on imported oil | Response: more domestic oil, energy efficiency

say.text: Did the war cause the oil crisis? One account says the war shaped its timing more than its cause. OPEC already wanted higher prices, because the dollar was losing value.

show.text: The war shaped the timing more than the cause

say.text: A second oil shock came in 1979. In Iran, the Shah left on January 16, and Ayatollah Khomeini landed in Tehran on February 1.

show.text: 1979 Jan 16: Shah leaves Iran; 1979 Feb 1: Khomeini returns

say.text: The Iranian revolution was at the heart of that second crisis.
There was one big peace deal too. President Carter hosted Egypt's Sadat and Israel's Begin at Camp David for 13 days.
They signed frameworks on September 17, 1978. The Egypt-Israel peace treaty followed on March 26, 1979. It was the first peace treaty between Israel and any Arab neighbor.

show.text: 1978 Sept 17: frameworks signed; 1979 March 26: peace treaty

ask.q: Why is the 1979 Egypt-Israel treaty considered historic?
ask.right: It was the first peace treaty between Israel and any of its Arab neighbors
ask.why: The treaty followed the 1978 Camp David Accords and was the first of its kind between Israel and an Arab neighbor.

say.text: Sadat and Begin shared the 1978 Nobel Peace Prize. Yet the accords did not bring an immediate end to hostilities, and their legacy is debated.
Not all change came from wars. The last story is about two movements. The sources we use tell the American story, so we will too.
In 1962, Rachel Carson published Silent Spring. It described the harm pesticides like DDT did to birds.
Before 1970 a factory could legally dump pollution. There was no EPA, and the strong Clean Air and Clean Water laws of 1970 and 1972 did not yet exist.

show.text: No EPA; no Clean Air Act; no Clean Water Act

say.text: Senator Gaylord Nelson saw that the anti-war protests had shown the public could mobilize in huge numbers. So he organized Earth Day.
About 20 million Americans took part. That was roughly 10 percent of the whole population.
President Nixon proposed a new agency, the Environmental Protection Agency, and Congress let his plan take effect. Its official birthday is December 2, 1970.

show.text: 1970 April 22: first Earth Day; 1970 Dec 2: EPA established

ask.q: What came shortly after the first Earth Day in 1970?
ask.right: The US Environmental Protection Agency was created
wrong: The Paris Peace Accords were signed
ask.why: After the first Earth Day in April 1970, the EPA was established that December.

say.text: Some environmental justice activists add another view. They say the Earth Day movement was largely led by white people focused on conserving wild areas. The civil rights movement had already faced environmental unfairness for years.
Meanwhile, second-wave feminism grew in the US from the 1960s through the 1970s. It sought equal rights and more freedom in politics, work, family and sexuality.
The National Organization for Women formed in 1966. Wins included the Equal Pay Act of 1963, Title IX in 1972, and Roe v. Wade in 1973.

show.text: 1963: Equal Pay Act; 1966: NOW formed; 1972: Title IX; 1973: Roe v. Wade

say.text: Title IX banned sex discrimination in education programs that receive federal funding.

ask.right: It banned sex discrimination in education programs that receive federal funding
ask.why: Title IX of 1972 banned sex-based discrimination in federally funded education programs.

say.text: The Equal Rights Amendment passed Congress on March 22, 1972, but was never ratified. The movement also argued over issues like abortion.
Women of color played major roles in the civil rights movement. But they were not offered the same opportunities as their white counterparts.
Here is what else was happening, year by year, as a frame of reference.

show.text: 1966: Cultural Revolution launched; NOW formed. 1967: Six-Day War. 1968: Tet; Prague Spring; Paris May. 1970: Earth Day; EPA. 1972: Title IX. 1973: Paris Accords; Yom Kippur War; oil embargo. 1975: Saigon falls. 1976: Mao dies. 1978-79: Camp David; Iranian revolution

say.text: One last check, to pull it together.

ask.q: Which pair of events happened in 1973?
ask.right: The Yom Kippur War and the Arab oil embargo
wrong: The Tet Offensive and the Prague Spring
The first Earth Day and the creation of the EPA
The Camp David Accords and the Egypt-Israel peace treaty
ask.why: The Yom Kippur War and the embargo were in October 1973. Tet and Prague were 1968, Earth Day and the EPA 1970, and Camp David 1978 to 1979.

say.text: These years brought war, protest, oil shocks and new movements. Next time, class 59: 20th-century science and technology.

frame_of_reference.elsewhere: Mao launched the Cultural Revolution in China, and the National Organization for Women formed in the United States.
The Six-Day War was fought June 5-10, while China's Red Guard phase was under way.
Tet began January 31. Dubcek took over Czechoslovakia's Communist Party on January 5. Paris protests started in May, and the US Civil Rights Act of 1968 was signed.
The National Environmental Policy Act was signed January 1. The first Earth Day was April 22. The EPA was established December 2.
Title IX became law, and Congress passed the Equal Rights Amendment on March 22.

The Paris Peace Accords were signed January 27, and Roe v. Wade was decided. The Yom Kippur War began October 6, and the oil embargo began October 17. Kissinger and Le Duc Tho won the Nobel Peace Prize.
Saigon fell on April 30. Hubert van Es photographed the helicopter evacuation on April 29.
Mao died September 9, and the Gang of Four was arrested in October. TIME magazine named American women its 'Women of the Year'.
Camp David Accords were signed September 17, 1978. The Shah left Iran January 16, 1979, and Khomeini returned February 1. The Egypt-Israel treaty was signed March 26, 1979.

other_side.claim: The Cultural Revolution killed about 1.6 million people (Walder's estimate, for 1966-1969).
other_side.other_view: Published estimates range from about 40,000 to 8 million. Walder says the low ones come from official party statements, and the high ones from angry guesses. Other historians such as Song Yongyi say probably 2 to 3 million. Britannica gives 500,000 to 2 million. Exact numbers are uncertain because scholars cannot freely reach state records.

other_side.claim: The Gang of Four was responsible for the Cultural Revolution's excesses.
other_side.other_view: After Mao's death the Gang was blamed and Jiang Qing was convicted. But it remains unclear which major decisions came from Mao and which from the Gang's own planning. Britannica says Mao launched the movement.

other_side.claim: Israel's 1967 strike was a preemptive defence against an approaching Arab attack.
other_side.other_view: Israel's foreign minister Abba Eban later wrote that Nasser did not want war. Military historian Martin van Creveld argued that Israel's forces were ready to provoke one.

other_side.claim: The Yom Kippur War caused the 1973 oil crisis.
other_side.other_view: One account says the war shaped the timing of the crisis more than its cause. OPEC had already wanted higher prices, because the dollar was losing value.

other_side.claim: Earth Day launched the modern environmental movement in the US.
other_side.other_view: Some environmental justice activists say the early movement was largely led by white people focused on conserving wild areas. They say the civil rights movement had faced environmental unfairness for years.

other_side.claim: The Camp David Accords were a lasting breakthrough for Middle East peace.
other_side.other_view: The accords did not bring an immediate end to hostilities, and historians debate their long-term impact. The Office of the Historian calls the 1979 treaty the high-water mark of the peace process under Carter.
